The year is 216 BC. The Second Punic War is in full swing. Hannibal Barca has, to the amazement of the entire mediterranean world, crossed the alps with an army 50 thousand men (and about forty elephants) strong, and has soundly crushed the romans in battle twice already, humiliating them and nearly wiping out their army. For this very reason, the dictator (Quick aside; in Rome, this was an elective office given to one man to undertake decisive action unburdened by the slow democratic process) for the previous year, Quintus Fabius, had pursued what we now know as Fabian tactics; he shadowed Hannibal, but did not let himself be drawn to an engagement where the Carthaginian general would have an advantage. This was what Hannibal was best at, so this is what Hannibal would not be allowed to do.

But the people of Rome are beyond proud, and they saw this decision as cowardice, not caution. So they dismissed Fabius and raised a vast army over 80 thousand men strong, led by two consuls,Varro and Paullus (Another aside; consuls in Rome were like president, but also generals, but much more). They usually lead armies independently, but in these dangerous and unusual times, the senate has decided that they would both co-command the single, vast force to defeat Hannibal once and for all. The nature of their co-command? Paullus would lead one day, then Varro the next, then back to Paullus, et cetera; thus is the stage set for the largest battle of the Second Punic War.

The two opposing armies meet each other and set up their fortified camps, facing one another, on the Apulian plain, near the town of Cannae. A scant few miles separate them. A day passes. Paullus is in command. Hannibal forms up to give battle, but Paullus will not be drawn into an engagement, knowing the flat terrain favours the Carthaginian and his famed Numidian cavalry. The Romans can afford to wait for Hannibal to get tired and leave, and fight him later, in more favourable conditions. But the next day, Varrus is in command, and he wants a battle, and glory, and cavalry be damned; Rome's legions are the best heavy infantry in the world, after all. Why shy away from battle, especially given Rome's numerical superiority?

So both armies formed. And what happened next, can scarcely be described. From wiki (paraphrased):

As the armies advanced on one another, Hannibal gradually extended the center of his line. Polybius described the weak Carthaginian center as deployed in a crescent, curving out toward the Romans in the middle with the African troops on their flanks in echelon formation. On the flanks of the battle, the Carthaginian cavalry drove off its Roman counterpart. After this, the masses of infantry on both sides advanced towards each other in the center of the field. Hannibal stood with his men in the weak center and held them to a controlled retreat. The crescent of Hispanic and Gallic troops buckled inwards as they gradually withdrew. Knowing the superiority of the Roman infantry, Hannibal had instructed his infantry to withdraw deliberately, creating an even tighter semicircle around the attacking Roman forces. By doing so, he had turned the strength of the Roman infantry into a weakness. While the front ranks were gradually advancing, the bulk of the Roman troops began to lose their cohesion, as they began crowding themselves into the growing gap. Soon they were compacted together so closely that they had little space to wield their weapons. In pressing so far forward in their desire to destroy the retreating and seemingly collapsing line of Hispanic and Gallic troops, the Romans had ignored (possibly due to the dust) the African troops that stood uncommitted on the projecting ends of this now-reversed crescent. This also gave the Carthaginian cavalry time to attack the Roman center in the rear. The Roman infantry, now stripped of protection on both its flanks, formed a wedge that drove deeper and deeper into the Carthaginian semicircle, driving itself into an alley formed by the African infantry on the wings. At this decisive point, Hannibal ordered his African infantry to turn inwards and advance against the Roman flanks, creating an encirclement in one of the earliest known examples of a pincer movement. Polybius wrote, "as their outer ranks were continually cut down, and the survivors forced to pull back and huddle together, they were finally all killed where they stood."

The entire Roman Army was destroyed. And the moral of the story is: let your armies be led firmly, and by a single man, for two generals fighting each other in your rear is worse than ten thousand men fighting you from up front.

Oh; and also: Don't fight Hannibal. You will lose.
